title: The Kit and Seven Stitches
bigQuestion: How does one needle and one piece of thread hold fabric together in seven different ways?

story.title: One Square, Seven Rows
story.kicker: Jonah thought sewing was one thing. His practice square proved it was at least seven.
paragraphs: On the first day of the textiles unit, Ms. Okafor handed every student a six-inch square of plain cotton, a needle, a card of pins and a spool of red thread. "Red so you can see your mistakes," she said. Jonah turned the needle over in his fingers. It was a lot smaller than he expected, and the hole at the end looked impossible.

It took him four tries to get the thread through the eye. On the fifth try he wet the end of the thread, pinched it flat and pushed it through. Ms. Okafor showed the class how to roll a knot at the tail, and Jonah's first knot slid straight off the end of the thread. His second one held.

The square had seven pencil lines drawn across it. "One line, one stitch," Ms. Okafor said. "By Friday you will know all seven by name, and you will know which one to reach for." The first line was the running stitch: in, out, in, out, like a dashed line. Jonah's stitches started tiny and grew bigger and bigger as he hurried. When he pulled the thread tight, the fabric bunched up like a curtain.

"That is tension," Ms. Okafor said, smoothing the cotton flat. "Not too loose, not too tight. Let the thread lie in the fabric, not fight it." Jonah tried the second line more slowly. The stitches came out closer to the same size, and the square stayed flat.

By Friday the square had seven rows: running, basting, back, whip, slip, blanket and overcast. Some rows were crooked. The blanket stitch on the edge looked like a row of little fence posts, and it was the one Jonah was proudest of. Ms. Okafor held the square up to the window so the light came through the thread. "Keep this," she said. "Next week you will fix a real seam, and you will want to remember which stitch does what."
story.think: Jonah's first row of running stitches got bigger as he hurried and bunched the fabric when he pulled. What two things went wrong, and what would you tell him to change?

lessons.title: Tools in the Kit
lessons.mainIdea: A basic hand-sewing kit has a small set of tools, and each one has a job that no other tool does as well.
reading: Open a small sewing kit and lay everything out on the table. You will find needles, thread, straight pins, a *pincushion*, small sharp scissors, a *thimble*, a tape measure and a *seam ripper*. Before you can sew anything, you need to know what each tool does and why it earns its place in the box.

Needles carry the thread through the fabric. Thread is the line that holds the pieces together. Straight pins hold two layers of fabric in place before you stitch, so the layers cannot slide apart. The pincushion is a small stuffed pad where pins and needles live when they are not in your hand. A pin left on a chair or the floor ends up in someone's foot.

Scissors in a sewing kit are for thread and fabric only. Cutting paper with them dulls the blades, and dull scissors chew fabric instead of cutting it. A tape measure is a soft ruler that bends around a body or a curve. A seam ripper is a small hook with a sharp inside edge that slides under a stitch and cuts it, so you can undo a mistake without cutting the fabric.

The thimble is the tool people skip, and then their fingertip pays for it. It is a small metal or rubber cap worn on the middle finger of the hand that holds the needle. When you push the needle through thick fabric, you push with the thimble, not with bare skin. Every tool goes back in the kit when you are done, and every pin gets counted.

words.d: a small cap worn on the middle finger to push the needle through fabric
a small stuffed pad that holds pins and needles safely when not in use
a small hooked tool with a sharp inside edge that cuts stitches without cutting fabric

look.title: The Kit on the Table
look.text: A kit is dumped on a desk: three needles loose in the bottom of the box, a spool of thread, a pair of scissors with tape stuck to the blades from a poster project, a tape measure, and no pincushion. A student says, "Everything is here, let's start."
look.prompt: Name two problems with this kit and say what could go wrong with each before the first stitch is sewn.

check.q: What is the thimble for?
choices: Holding pins when they are not in use
Pushing the needle through fabric without hurting your finger
Measuring around a curve
Cutting thread close to the fabric
check.why: A thimble caps the middle finger so you can push the needle through thick fabric without piercing your skin.

check.q: Why should sewing scissors never be used to cut paper?
choices: Paper is too thin to cut
Paper leaves ink on the blades
Paper dulls the blades, and dull scissors chew fabric
Paper makes the scissors rust
check.why: Cutting paper dulls the blades. Dull scissors do not cut fabric cleanly; they chew and fray it.

check.q: A student wants to undo a crooked row of stitches without damaging the fabric. Which tool does that job?
choices: Straight pins
The tape measure
The thimble
The seam ripper
check.why: A seam ripper slides under a stitch and cuts the thread with its inside edge, leaving the fabric whole.

lessons.title: Needle Sizes and Thread
lessons.mainIdea: Hand needles are numbered so that a bigger number means a finer needle, and the needle and thread should match the fabric.
reading: Pick up a packet of hand needles and read the label: "Sharps, sizes 3 to 9." The word tells you the type, and the numbers tell you the size. Here is the rule that surprises people: with hand needles, a bigger number means a thinner, shorter needle. A size 3 sharp is thick and long, good for denim. A size 9 is fine and short, good for thin cotton.

The needle you choose should match the fabric. A thick needle on thin fabric leaves visible holes. A thin needle on heavy fabric bends or snaps when you push. Most classroom kits use *sharps*, an all-purpose needle with a round eye and a sharp point, in a middle size such as 7. Embroidery needles have a longer eye for thicker thread. Ballpoint needles have a rounded tip that slips between the loops of a knit instead of piercing them.

Thread matters as much as the needle. All-purpose polyester or cotton-polyester thread works for almost everything in this unit. It is strong, it does not stretch much, and it comes in every color. Match the color to the fabric for a repair you want to hide. Choose a contrasting color for practice so you can see every stitch. Look at the thread against the *eye* of the needle: the thread must pass through the eye without being forced.

One more number matters: length. Cut a piece of thread about 18 inches long, roughly from your fingertips to your elbow. Longer thread tangles and knots on itself while you sew. Shorter thread runs out before the seam is done. If a job needs more, you can always knot off and start a new piece.

words.d: all-purpose hand needles with a round eye and a sharp point
the hole at the top of a needle that the thread passes through
polyester or cotton-polyester thread strong enough for most hand and machine sewing

look.title: Hand Needle Sizes
look.cite: Common hand-needle sizing; higher number = finer needle
look.prompt: A student is mending a pair of jeans and reaches for a size 10 needle. What will probably happen, and which size fits better?

check.q: In hand-needle sizes, what does a bigger number mean?
choices: A thinner, shorter needle
A thicker, longer needle
A needle with a bigger eye
A needle for knits only
check.why: Hand needles are numbered so that the larger the size number, the finer and shorter the needle.

check.q: Why is about 18 inches a good length of thread to cut?
choices: It is the length of a spool
Longer thread tangles and shorter thread runs out too soon
It is the only length the knot will hold
It matches the size of the needle eye
check.why: About 18 inches, fingertip to elbow, is long enough to finish a seam but short enough not to tangle.

check.q: Which needle is designed to slip between the loops of a knit fabric instead of piercing them?
choices: A sharp
An embroidery needle
A ballpoint needle
A size 3 needle
check.why: Ballpoint needles have a rounded tip that pushes between knit loops without cutting them.

lessons.title: Thread the Needle, Tie the Knot
lessons.mainIdea: Cut the thread at an angle, pass it through the eye, and roll a knot on the tail so the first stitch cannot pull through.
reading: Sit near a window or a lamp and hold the needle in one hand with the eye up. Cut the thread with sharp scissors at a slight angle, so the end is clean and pointed. Do not bite it or break it; a frayed end will not go through. Wet the tip of the thread on your lip, pinch it flat between your thumb and finger so only a tiny point shows, and push that point through the eye. If it will not go, cut a fresh end and try again.

Pull about 4 inches through the eye so the thread does not slip back out. For most work you will sew with a *single thread*: one strand through the fabric, with a knot on the long tail only. For a button or a seam that takes strain, pull the ends even and knot both together to sew with a *double thread*, which is twice as strong.

Now the knot. Hold the tail of the thread between your thumb and first finger. Wrap the thread once around the tip of your first finger, roll the loop off your finger with your thumb so it twists, then pinch and pull the loop down to the end of the thread. It tightens into a small knot. If the knot slides off the end, you rolled it too close to the tip. Leave about half an inch of tail.

Test the knot before you sew. Push the needle into the fabric from the back and pull until the knot stops against the cloth. If the knot pops through the weave, the fabric is loose or the knot is too small; tie a second knot on top of the first. A knot that holds is the difference between a seam and a piece of thread lying on the cloth.

words.d: sewing with one strand through the eye and a knot on the long tail only
sewing with both ends of the thread pulled even and knotted together for extra strength

look.title: Five Tries at the Eye
look.text: Maria bites off a piece of thread, pushes the fuzzy end at the eye four times, and misses. She wets it, pinches it flat, and it goes through on the fifth try. She pulls one inch through, rolls a knot right at the very tip of the thread, and the knot falls off. Put in order what she should do differently, from cutting to knotting.
look.prompt: List the three changes that would have saved Maria four tries and one lost knot.

check.q: Why does a bitten or broken thread end refuse to go through the eye?
choices: It is too long
It is too wet
It is too strong
It is frayed and spreads out instead of forming a point
check.why: A clean angled cut makes a point. A frayed end fans out and cannot pass through a small eye.

check.q: When should you sew with a double thread?
choices: For a button or any seam that takes strain
For every stitch, always
Only for basting
Only when the fabric is thin
check.why: Doubling the thread makes it twice as strong, which matters for buttons and seams that get pulled.

check.q: A knot keeps sliding off the end of the thread. What went wrong?
choices: The thread is too thick
The knot was rolled too close to the tip, with no tail left
The needle eye is too small
The thread was not wet enough
check.why: Roll the knot with about half an inch of tail below it, or the loop tightens on nothing and slips off.

lessons.title: Pins, Needles and Safe Hands
lessons.mainIdea: Sharp tools stay in the pincushion, get counted, and are passed handle-first so that nobody gets hurt.
reading: Picture a table with six students, thirty pins and six needles. By the end of class every one of those sharp points has to be found. Start with a count: know how many pins you took out, and put every one back in the pincushion, point in, before you leave. A pin in a carpet or a couch cushion waits for a bare foot or a hand. A needle dropped on the floor is nearly invisible.

Never put pins or needles in your mouth, even for a second while your hands are busy. People do it without thinking, and a breath or a laugh can pull a pin into the throat. Keep the pincushion within reach and use it. When you pin fabric, push the pin in and out of the cloth so the point is buried in the fabric, and pin across the seam line, not along it, so the pins are easy to pull out as you sew.

Pass scissors closed, with the handles toward the other person and the blades in your own hand. Pass a needle stuck in a scrap of fabric or in the pincushion, never loose. Cut away from your body. If you prick your finger, stop, wash the spot with soap and water, cover it with a bandage, and tell the teacher. Do not keep sewing on light fabric with a bleeding finger.

A bent pin or needle goes in the trash, not back in the cushion; it will bend again and can snap. Snapped points get wrapped in tape before they are thrown out. These rules take about ten seconds a class. A pin in a foot takes a lot longer.

words.d: a thin metal pin with a point on one end and a head on the other, used to hold fabric layers together
placing pins at a right angle to the seam line so they are easy to remove while sewing

look.title: Counting Pins at the Bell
look.text: The bell is about to ring. Dev has three pins in his mouth, two stuck in the sleeve of his hoodie, and a bent needle he tossed back in the pincushion. His pincushion started with twenty pins and now shows fourteen. He says, "I'll find the rest tomorrow."
look.prompt: Find every unsafe choice in this scene and say what Dev should do in the next two minutes.

check.q: Why should pins be placed across the seam line instead of along it?
choices: It uses fewer pins
It keeps the fabric from fraying
They are easy to pull out as you sew, and they hold the layers square
It hides the pins from view
check.why: Pins set at a right angle to the seam hold the layers in place and slide out easily as the needle approaches.

check.q: What should you do with a bent needle?
choices: Straighten it and keep using it
Put it back in the pincushion for later
Leave it on the table
Throw it away, wrapped if the point is broken
check.why: A bent needle will bend again and can snap. It goes in the trash, with a broken point taped so it cannot cut anyone.

check.q: Which is the safe way to hand scissors to a classmate?
choices: Closed, handles toward the classmate
Open, so they can grab the handle
Tossed gently onto the table in front of them
Blades first, so you keep the handle
check.why: Closed scissors passed handle-first keep the blades in your own hand and away from the other person.

lessons.title: The Running Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The running stitch is the simplest stitch, a dashed line of even stitches used for gathering, light seams and hand quilting.
reading: Thread a needle with a single thread, knot the tail, and bring the needle up from the back of the fabric on your pencil line. Now push the tip of the needle down through the fabric about 1/8 inch ahead, then up again 1/8 inch after that, and down again. You can load two or three stitches on the needle before you pull the thread through. That in-and-out motion is the *running stitch*. From the front it looks like a dashed line.

The goal is even stitches, all the same length, with the same gap between them. Beginners make the stitches grow as they speed up, and the row looks like Morse code. Slow down and watch the needle tip, not your hand. Pull the thread through until it lies flat in the cloth. If the fabric puckers, you pulled too hard; ease it back.

Where does the running stitch belong? It is fast, so it is used for *gathering*: sew a long running stitch along an edge, then pull the thread and the fabric bunches into soft folds, the way a skirt gathers into a waistband. It works for light seams that will not take strain and for hand quilting, where tiny running stitches hold three layers together. It is not the stitch for a seam that gets pulled every day, because the thread can slide.

End the row on the back of the fabric. Take a tiny stitch in place, pass the needle through the loop before you pull it tight, and repeat once. That is a finishing knot. Trim the thread to about a quarter inch. Now hold the row up to the light and look at the spacing. That is the first line on your practice square.

words.d: a simple in-and-out stitch that looks like a dashed line, used for gathering, light seams and quilting
pulling a row of running stitches so the fabric bunches into soft folds

look.title: Reading a Row of Stitches
look.text: Three practice squares are on the table. Square A has stitches that are tiny at the start and half an inch long at the end. Square B has even stitches but the fabric is bunched into a ridge. Square C has even stitches and lies flat, but there is no knot and the thread has slid halfway out.
look.prompt: Diagnose each square: what did the sewer do wrong, and what is the one fix for each?

check.q: What does a running stitch look like from the front of the fabric?
choices: A solid line
A dashed line
A row of loops over the edge
A row of crosses
check.why: The running stitch goes in and out of the fabric, leaving a line of dashes with gaps between them.

check.q: A row of running stitches has made the fabric pucker into a ridge. What happened?
choices: The needle was too small
The stitches were too even
The thread was pulled too tight
The thread was too short
check.why: Puckering means the tension was too tight. The thread should lie flat in the cloth, not pull it up.

check.q: Which job is the running stitch best for?
choices: A seam on the seat of a pair of pants
Attaching a button
Sewing over a raw edge to stop fraying
Gathering a skirt into folds
check.why: A long running stitch can be pulled to gather fabric. It is too weak for seams that take strain.

lessons.title: Basting: Stitches Meant to Leave
lessons.mainIdea: Basting is a long, loose running stitch that holds fabric in place temporarily and is pulled out after the real seam is sewn.
reading: Imagine you are hemming a pair of pants and you want to try them on before you sew the hem for good. Pins would scratch and fall out. Instead you *baste*: sew a running stitch with stitches about half an inch long, loosely, in a thread color that stands out. It takes a minute. The hem holds, you try the pants on, and if the length is right you sew the real hem next to the basting and pull the basting out.

Basting is a placeholder. Because it will be removed, there are rules that are the opposite of normal sewing. Use a bright, contrasting thread so you can find every stitch later. Do not knot the end tightly; a small loose knot or just a backstitch is enough. Keep the stitches long and the tension loose. Do not baste exactly on the seam line, or the permanent stitches will sew right over your basting and trap it.

Basting also holds slippery or bulky layers that pins cannot manage: a zipper before it is stitched in, a sleeve eased into an armhole, two layers of thick fleece. Tailors baste pockets and collars in place to check the position before committing. The stitch is temporary, but the habit is professional. It costs a minute now and saves a seam ripper session later.

To remove basting, snip the thread every few inches and pull the short pieces out with your fingers or tweezers. Never yank a long basting thread through a finished seam; it can pull and pucker the permanent stitches. Once the basting is out, press the seam and nobody will ever know it was there.

words.d: long, loose temporary stitches that hold fabric in place until the permanent seam is sewn
thread in a color that stands out from the fabric so it can be seen and removed easily

look.title: Basting a Hem to Try On
look.text: Put these steps in order for basting a pant hem: (a) try the pants on and check the length; (b) sew a long, loose running stitch in bright thread just below the fold; (c) fold the hem up and pin it; (d) sew the permanent hem; (e) snip and pull out the basting; (f) press the hem.
look.prompt: Write the letters in the right order and explain why the basting goes in before the trying-on, not after.

check.q: Why is basting done in a bright, contrasting thread?
choices: So the stitches are easy to see and remove later
Because bright thread is stronger
Because it matches most fabrics
So the seam looks decorative
check.why: Basting is temporary. A contrasting color lets you find every stitch when it is time to pull it out.

check.q: How should basting stitches compare to normal running stitches?
choices: Shorter and tighter
Exactly the same
Longer and looser
Doubled for strength
check.why: Basting stitches are long, about half an inch, and loose, because they only hold things in place for a while.

check.q: What is the safe way to remove a long line of basting from a finished seam?
choices: Pull the whole thread out from one end in one motion
Cut the fabric next to the basting
Leave it in; it will not show
Snip the thread every few inches and pull out the short pieces
check.why: Yanking a long thread can pucker the permanent stitches. Short snipped pieces slide out without pulling.

lessons.title: The Back Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The back stitch overlaps each stitch with the one before it, making the strongest hand seam and the closest thing to a machine stitch.
reading: A split seam on the side of a backpack needs a stitch that will not slide or pull apart. That is the *back stitch*. Bring the needle up from the back on the seam line. Take one stitch backward, about 1/8 inch, going down into the fabric. Now bring the needle up 1/8 inch ahead of where you first came up. Go back down into the hole at the end of the last stitch. Come up 1/8 inch ahead again. Each stitch goes back to meet the last one, so from the front the line is solid.

The secret is that the thread on the back of the fabric overlaps itself. Every stitch is locked by the one after it, so if one stitch breaks the seam does not unravel the way a running stitch would. It is slower than a running stitch because you pull the thread through after every single stitch, and that is exactly why it holds.

Use the back stitch for any seam that takes strain: the side seam of a bag, a split in the seat of pants, a strap, a toy that gets thrown. Keep the stitches small and even, 1/8 inch or less on medium fabric. A common mistake is skipping the backward step and going forward twice, which turns it into a running stitch with extra work. Another is coming up too far ahead, which leaves gaps in the solid line.

Use double thread for a seam that will be pulled hard. Finish with two small stitches in place on the back and trim. Compare this row to your running stitch row and tug on both. The running stitch slides. The back stitch does not.

words.d: a stitch that returns to the end of the previous stitch, making a solid, strong line
the line where two pieces of fabric are stitched together

look.title: Which Row Would You Trust?
look.text: Two students each mended the split side seam of a canvas tote bag. Ava used a running stitch with single thread. Ben used a back stitch with double thread. The bag is loaded with six textbooks and carried up three flights of stairs, ten times.
look.prompt: Predict what happens to each mend and explain why, using what you know about how each stitch is locked.

check.q: In a back stitch, where does the needle go down on each new stitch?
choices: Ahead of the last stitch, leaving a gap
Into the hole at the end of the previous stitch
Through the same hole it came up from
Over the raw edge of the fabric
check.why: Each back stitch returns to the end of the last stitch, which is why the line is solid and locked.

check.q: Why does a back-stitched seam hold when one stitch breaks?
choices: The thread is thicker
It is sewn with a larger needle
Each stitch overlaps and locks the one before it
The stitches are farther apart
check.why: The overlapping thread on the back locks every stitch, so one broken stitch does not unravel the row.

check.q: A student's "back stitch" row looks like a dashed line. What did they most likely do?
choices: Used thread that was too thin
Pulled the thread too tight
Sewed with a ballpoint needle
Skipped the backward step and only went forward
check.why: Going forward twice without returning to the last stitch produces a running stitch, which leaves gaps.

lessons.title: The Whip Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The whip stitch wraps thread over the edge of two pieces of fabric to join them quickly, and it shows on the outside.
reading: Two felt pieces need to be joined edge to edge to make a small pouch. Line the edges up and hold them together. Bring the needle up through both layers near the edge, from the back, so the knot is hidden between the layers. Now carry the thread over the top of the edge and push the needle through both layers from the back again, about 1/8 inch along. Pull. Repeat. Each stitch wraps over the edge on a slant. That is the *whip stitch*.

The whip stitch is fast and it holds edges together well, but it is visible: the slanted stitches lie on the outside of the seam. On felt, fleece and other fabrics that do not fray, the visible stitches are part of the look. Craft projects, stuffed toys and appliqué use it on purpose, often in a contrasting color.

Keep the stitches the same distance from the edge and the same distance apart, or the slant will wobble. If you pull too hard the edge rolls over and the seam gets a lump. If you go too far from the edge you use extra thread and the join gets bulky. On a woven fabric that frays, the whip stitch alone is not enough for a seam that takes strain; the threads of the fabric can pull out under the stitches.

The whip stitch is also the quick fix for a small hole in a knit sock or the closing stitch on a stuffed toy after you fill it. Bring the edges together, whip over them, knot inside, and done. It is the stitch you reach for when the join must be quick and does not have to be invisible.

words.d: a stitch that wraps over the edge of two layers on a slant, joining them quickly
when threads at a cut edge of woven fabric work loose and come apart

look.title: Two Edges, One Stitch
look.text: A student is closing the last edge of a stuffed felt heart. She brings the needle up through both layers, carries the thread over the edge, and comes up again a quarter inch along. Halfway across, she pulls hard and the edge rolls into a ridge. She finishes the seam with the knot on the outside.
look.prompt: Name the two mistakes and describe how each stitch should have been made instead.

check.q: How is the thread carried in a whip stitch?
choices: Over the edge of the fabric on a slant
Straight along the seam line
Backward into the last stitch
Under a folded hem where it cannot be seen
check.why: The whip stitch wraps the thread over the edge with each stitch, leaving slanted stitches on the outside.

check.q: On which fabric does a whip stitch work best for a visible seam?
choices: Loosely woven linen
Felt, which does not fray
Silk
Fine cotton that frays easily
check.why: Felt and fleece do not fray, so the visible whip stitches hold cleanly and become part of the design.

check.q: A whip-stitched edge rolled into a lump. What most likely caused it?
choices: The stitches were too far apart
The fabric was too thick
The thread was pulled too tight
The knot was between the layers
check.why: Pulling the wrapped thread too hard rolls the edge over. Ease the tension so the edge stays flat.

lessons.title: The Slip Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The slip stitch hides inside a fold so a hem or an opening is closed with almost nothing showing on the outside.
reading: Look at the hem of a good pair of dress pants: you can barely find a stitch. That is a *slip stitch*, sometimes called a blind stitch. Fold the hem up and press it. Anchor the knot inside the fold where it cannot be seen. Slide the needle along inside the fold for about 1/4 inch and bring it out. Now pick up just one or two threads of the outer fabric, right beside where the needle came out. Slide the needle back into the fold and travel another 1/4 inch. Repeat.

From the outside you see only a tiny dot where the needle caught the outer fabric. From the inside you see the thread traveling hidden in the fold. Most of the thread is never visible, which is why the stitch is nearly invisible. The trade-off is strength: a slip stitch is not for seams that take strain. It is for hems, for closing the opening in a pillow after stuffing, and for attaching linings.

The two mistakes that show are picking up too much of the outer fabric, which makes a visible dash on the front, and pulling too tight, which makes a dimple on every stitch. Catch one or two threads, not a bite of cloth, and let the thread lie easy. Match the thread color to the fabric; on the front the color is what hides the dot.

Practice on your square by folding one edge over 1/2 inch, pressing it, and slip stitching along it. Then flip the square and look at the front. If you can see a row of dots and nothing more, you have it. If you can see dashes, you caught too much.

words.d: a nearly invisible stitch that travels inside a fold and catches one or two threads of the outer fabric
the finished bottom edge of a garment, folded up and stitched

look.title: Front and Back of a Hem
look.text: Turn a hemmed pant leg inside out and you see a thread running along inside a fold, coming out every quarter inch to catch the outer fabric. Turn it right side out and you see nothing but a row of dots the size of a pinpoint, in thread the same navy as the pants. Now imagine the same hem sewn with red thread, catching a quarter inch of fabric at each stitch.
look.prompt: Describe what the second hem would look like from the front and name the two things the sewer did wrong.

check.q: Where does most of the thread travel in a slip stitch?
choices: Over the raw edge
On the front of the fabric
Inside the fold of the hem
In the seam allowance of a back stitch
check.why: The slip stitch hides the thread inside the fold, surfacing only to catch a thread or two of the outer fabric.

check.q: Which job is the slip stitch best suited for?
choices: A side seam on a bag
Closing the opening of a stuffed pillow so it cannot be seen
Sewing on a button
Gathering a skirt
check.why: The slip stitch is for closings and hems where looks matter more than strength.

check.q: A slip-stitched hem shows a row of dimples on the front. What went wrong?
choices: The thread color did not match
The stitches were too far apart
The needle was too thin
The thread was pulled too tight
check.why: Pulling a slip stitch tight puckers the outer fabric at each catch. The thread should lie easy.

lessons.title: The Blanket Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The blanket stitch finishes an edge with a row of upright stitches linked by a line of thread along the edge, and it can also be decorative.
reading: The edge of a fleece blanket, a felt bookmark or an appliqué shape often has a row of stitches that look like little fence posts joined by a rail along the edge. That is the *blanket stitch*. Hold the fabric with the edge toward you. Bring the needle up from the back, right at the edge, so the knot is hidden. Push the needle down through the fabric about 1/4 inch in from the edge and 1/4 inch along, but before you pull it through, catch the loop of thread under the needle tip. Pull. The thread hooks around itself at the edge, forming one post and one piece of rail.

Repeat: down 1/4 inch in and 1/4 inch along, thread under the needle, pull. The posts stand up from the edge and the rail runs along it. Even spacing is the whole game, so many sewers mark dots along the edge first with a fabric pencil. The posts should be the same height and the same distance apart.

The blanket stitch does two jobs. On a raw edge of fleece or wool it keeps the edge neat and adds a border. Around an appliqué, a shape sewn onto a background, it holds the shape down and outlines it. Done in a thick, colorful thread it becomes decoration. Common mistakes: forgetting to catch the loop under the needle, which turns the stitch into a plain whip stitch, and pulling so hard the rail cuts into the edge.

Turning a corner: at the corner, make three stitches into the same hole, fanning them out like the spokes of a wheel. Then continue along the next edge. Finish by taking the last stitch to the back and knotting it. Hold your practice square up. If the edge has a clean line of posts and a straight rail, you have it.

words.d: an edge stitch that makes upright stitches joined by a line of thread along the edge
a fabric shape sewn onto a background fabric as decoration

look.title: Posts and a Rail
look.text: Picture the edge of a gray felt bookmark with yellow thread. Every quarter inch a short yellow post stands straight up from the edge, and a single yellow line runs along the edge connecting the bottom of each post. At the corner, three posts fan out from one point.
look.prompt: Explain what the sewer must do with the thread under the needle to make the rail, and what the stitch would look like if they forgot.

check.q: What must you do before pulling each blanket stitch through?
choices: Catch the loop of thread under the needle tip
Tie a knot
Pull the thread out of the eye
Go back into the last stitch
check.why: Catching the loop under the needle makes the thread hook around itself at the edge, forming the rail.

check.q: What does the blanket stitch look like along an edge?
choices: A dashed line
A solid line
Upright posts joined by a line along the edge
A row of slanted wraps
check.why: Each stitch is an upright post; the thread caught at the edge forms a rail connecting them.

check.q: How do you turn a corner with the blanket stitch?
choices: Cut the thread and start over on the new edge
Skip the corner and continue on the next edge
Switch to a whip stitch for the corner
Make three stitches into the same hole, fanned out
check.why: Three stitches fanned from one corner hole carry the rail around the corner without a gap.

lessons.title: The Overcast Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The overcast stitch wraps thread over a raw edge to stop woven fabric from fraying.
reading: Cut a strip of woven cotton and rub the cut edge between your fingers. Threads come loose; that is *fraying*. Left alone, a raw edge inside a garment can fray until the seam itself pulls apart. Before sewing machines had a zigzag, sewers protected every raw edge by hand with the *overcast stitch*. Bring the needle up from the back about 1/4 inch from the edge. Carry the thread over the edge and come up from the back again, about 1/4 inch along. Each stitch is a slanted wrap around the edge.

That description sounds like the whip stitch, and the hand motion is the same. The difference is the job. The whip stitch joins two pieces. The overcast stitch wraps one raw edge, or the two raw edges of a seam allowance, to hold the loose threads in place. The stitches are usually a bit longer and more evenly slanted, and they should not pull the edge tight or it will roll.

Inside a skirt you might find the seam sewn with a back stitch and then both raw edges overcast together. That is a seam finish. It is not glamorous work, and nobody sees it, but the skirt lasts years longer. On fabric that frays badly, such as loosely woven linen, make the stitches closer. On tight fabric like poplin, 1/4 inch apart is plenty.

Fleece, felt and knits do not fray, so they do not need overcasting. Wovens do. Look at the inside seams of what you are wearing: many have a machine version of this stitch, a zigzag or a serged edge with three threads. The hand overcast is the ancestor of all of them. It is the seventh row on your square.

words.d: slanted stitches wrapped over a raw edge to keep woven fabric from fraying
the strip of fabric between the cut edge and the seam line
any treatment of a raw seam edge that stops it from fraying

look.title: Which Edges Need It?
look.text: Four projects are on the table: a fleece scarf with cut edges, a cotton drawstring bag with a back-stitched side seam, a felt pouch joined with a whip stitch, and a linen napkin with raw edges. One student wants to overcast every edge on every project to be safe.
look.prompt: Decide which projects need overcasting and which do not, and explain your reasoning for each.

check.q: What is the purpose of the overcast stitch?
choices: To join two pieces of felt
To keep a raw woven edge from fraying
To gather fabric into folds
To hide a hem
check.why: Overcasting wraps the raw edge so the fabric threads cannot work loose.

check.q: Which fabric does NOT need an overcast edge?
choices: Loosely woven linen
Cotton poplin
Fleece
Denim
check.why: Fleece, felt and knits do not fray. Woven fabrics like linen, poplin and denim do.

check.q: The whip stitch and the overcast stitch use the same motion. What is the difference?
choices: The overcast stitch uses a thicker needle
The whip stitch is only for hems
The overcast stitch goes backward each time
The whip stitch joins two pieces; the overcast stitch protects a raw edge
check.why: Same wrap, different job. Whip stitching joins; overcasting finishes a raw edge against fraying.

lessons.title: Stitch Length and Tension
lessons.mainIdea: Good hand sewing has stitches of even length and thread pulled just enough to lie flat, and both come from slowing down.
reading: Lay your practice square flat and look at your best row and your worst row side by side. The difference is almost always two things: *stitch length* and *tension*. Stitch length is how long each stitch is and how far apart the stitches are. Tension is how hard you pulled the thread. Neither one has a machine dial in hand sewing. Both come from your hands.

For length, choose a size for the job and keep it. Small stitches, about 1/8 inch or less, are stronger because there are more of them per inch and the fabric has more places to share the load. Long stitches, 1/4 to 1/2 inch, are faster and are right for basting and gathering. Whatever you choose, keep every stitch that length. Uneven stitches look sloppy and put more strain on the longest ones. If you struggle, draw a line and mark dots with a fabric pencil.

For tension, pull each stitch until the thread just lies flat, then stop. Too tight and the fabric puckers into ridges and the seam will not lie flat even after pressing. Too loose and the thread loops on the surface and the seam gapes when you tug it. A good test: run your finger along the seam. Ridges mean too tight. Loops you can lift with a fingernail mean too loose.

Most tension problems come from hurrying, and most length problems come from watching your hand instead of the needle tip. Slow down for the first ten stitches of any row and the rest tend to follow. Even stitches with even tension are the difference between a mend that looks like a mend and one that disappears.

words.d: the length of each stitch and the distance between stitches
how tightly the thread is pulled through the fabric
wrinkles or ridges in fabric caused by thread pulled too tight

look.title: Stitch Length by Job
look.prompt: Why are the strong seams at the small end of the table and the temporary stitches at the large end?

check.q: Which sign tells you the thread tension is too loose?
choices: Ridges along the seam
Thread loops on the surface you can lift with a fingernail
The needle bends
The knot pulls through the fabric
check.why: Loose tension leaves slack thread that loops above the fabric. Ridges mean tension that is too tight.

check.q: Why are small, even stitches stronger than a few long ones?
choices: They use less thread
They are easier to remove
More stitches per inch share the load across more places in the fabric
They are always sewn with double thread
check.why: Each stitch carries a share of the strain. More stitches per inch means less strain on any one stitch.

check.q: A student's stitches keep getting longer as the row goes on. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The thread is too long
The needle is too thick
The fabric is too thin
Speeding up and watching the hand instead of the needle tip
check.why: Hurrying is the usual cause of growing stitches. Slow down and watch where the needle tip enters.

lessons.title: Pressing as You Go
lessons.mainIdea: Pressing each seam with an iron before the next step makes sewing flatter, straighter and more accurate, and the iron is handled with care.
reading: A hem that was sewn without being folded and pressed first wanders up and down the leg. A seam that was never pressed sits in a lump. The habit that fixes both is *pressing* as you go: after each seam, before the next step, set the iron on it. Pressing is not ironing. Ironing slides the iron back and forth to remove wrinkles. Pressing lifts the iron, sets it down on the seam, holds for a few seconds, and lifts again. Sliding can stretch the fabric out of shape.

Set the iron to the setting for your fabric. Most irons mark cotton, wool, silk and synthetic settings, and the care label on the fabric or the bolt end tells you which. Too hot melts synthetics and scorches cotton. Test on a scrap first. To press a seam open, lay the seam face down, spread the two seam allowances apart with your fingers, and press along the line. To press a hem, fold it to the marked line, pin, and press the fold sharp before you stitch.

Iron safety is not optional. The plate of an iron reaches temperatures that burn skin on contact. Stand the iron on its heel when it is not in your hand. Keep the cord away from the edge of the board so nobody snags it. Never leave a hot iron face down, and never leave it on when you walk away. Unplug it at the end of the period. Steam is hot: keep your hand out of its path when you press.

The reward for pressing is precision. Pinning is easier on a pressed fold, stitches land where you aimed, and the finished project lies flat. Professionals say sewing is half pressing. On your practice square, press the slip-stitched fold and the seams, and notice how much neater everything looks.

words.d: setting a hot iron down on a seam and lifting it, without sliding, to flatten the fabric
pressing a seam so the two seam allowances lie flat on either side of the seam line

look.title: The Iron at the End of the Table
look.text: An iron is lying face down on the ironing board on the cotton setting, unplugged by nobody, with the cord hanging over the edge into the aisle. A student presses a polyester lining on that setting by sliding the iron back and forth. The lining puckers and shines. Another student reaches across the board and catches a puff of steam on the wrist.
look.prompt: List every unsafe or incorrect thing in this scene and say what the right practice is for each.

check.q: What is the difference between pressing and ironing?
choices: Pressing lifts and sets the iron down; ironing slides it
Pressing uses steam; ironing does not
Ironing is for seams; pressing is for wrinkles
There is no difference
check.why: Pressing is lift, set, hold, lift. Sliding the iron, as in ironing, can stretch a seam out of shape.

check.q: What should you do with the iron whenever it is not in your hand?
choices: Lay it face down on the board
Set it on the fabric so it stays warm
Stand it up on its heel
Hang it by the cord
check.why: An iron on its heel keeps the hot plate off the board and away from fabric and hands.

check.q: A polyester lining puckered and turned shiny under the iron. What most likely happened?
choices: The iron was too cold
The seam was pressed open
The fabric was pinned
The iron was set too hot for a synthetic fabric
check.why: Synthetics melt and shine at cotton temperatures. Use the synthetic setting and test on a scrap first.

review.q: Which stitch makes the strongest hand seam?
choices: Running stitch
Basting
Back stitch
Slip stitch
review.why: The back stitch overlaps and locks each stitch with the last, so it holds under strain.

review.q: A size 3 sharp compared to a size 9 sharp is:
choices: Thicker and longer
Thinner and shorter
The same size with a bigger eye
Only for knits
review.why: In hand needles, lower numbers are thicker and longer. Higher numbers are finer.

review.q: You need to close the stuffing opening on a cotton pillow so the stitches do not show. Which stitch?
choices: Whip stitch
Blanket stitch
Overcast stitch
Slip stitch
review.why: The slip stitch hides inside the fold and catches only a thread or two, so it is nearly invisible.

review.q: Which of these is a rule for basting?
choices: Use matching thread and tight knots
Use contrasting thread, long stitches and loose tension
Use double thread for strength
Baste exactly on the seam line
review.why: Basting is temporary, so it should be easy to see, easy to remove, and out of the way of the permanent seam.

review.q: Which stitch is used to stop the raw edge of woven fabric from fraying?
choices: Running stitch
Back stitch
Overcast stitch
Basting
review.why: Overcasting wraps thread over the raw edge to hold the loose fabric threads in place.

review.q: What is the safe rule about pins and your mouth?
choices: Only hold one pin at a time in your mouth
Hold pins in your lips, not your teeth
It is fine if you do not talk
Never put pins or needles in your mouth
review.why: A breath or a laugh can pull a pin into the throat. Pins live in the pincushion.

review.q: The blanket stitch differs from the whip stitch because:
choices: The thread is caught under the needle to form a rail along the edge
It is sewn from the back only
It uses a shorter needle
It cannot be used on felt
review.why: Catching the loop under the needle makes the rail that links the upright posts of the blanket stitch.

review.q: A seam puckers into ridges as you sew. What is the fix?
choices: Use a thicker thread
Ease the tension so the thread lies flat in the fabric
Make the stitches longer
Switch to a ballpoint needle
review.why: Ridges mean the thread was pulled too tight. Pull only until the thread lies flat.
